To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

the survival time of a motion picture in wide release at the box office is a function of the number of screens, the number of previews, the amount spent on advertising, the number of positive and negative critical reviews and the US box office performance of the film.

(1) the life-length of motion pictures at Australian box offices can be modelled using a Weibull distribution; (2) films that are previewed, receive more advertising, and are released on more screens at opening week are more likely to be successful in terms of their duration; (3) films that have higher US box office receipts, receive more positive critical reviews, and have more positive word-of-mouth demand are more likely to survive at the Australian box offices; (4) films
films that are previewed and have good opening-week performance have longer box office lives than other films.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the role of word-of-mouth in the survival of films at the box office.
how the survival of motion pictures can be understood as a function of word-of-mouth demand (as measured by consumer reviews) and adaptive supply (as measured by the number of screens).
the role of word-of-mouth and the supply of films in the Australian market.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the survival of a film is a function of its word-of-mouth demand, and its ability to adapt to this demand through the use of distributional strategies.
films with higher word-of-mouth intensity and more favourable critical reviews have greater survival probability at the box office.

the survival of motion pictures is determined by a complex set of interrelated factors that can be grouped into two broad categories: (1) the film itself and its characteristics, and (2) its distribution and performance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the Australian box office is not a market for lemons, but a market in which consumers can be confident that they will be able to make a good choice.

the Australian market for motion picture exhibition is a highly competitive one in which films that are successful at the US box office, that are previewed, that are well advertised, that receive positive reviews, and that open on a large number of screens are most likely to survive in Australia.
the survival of films at the box office depends on the strength of word-of-mouth, and the degree of adaptation of supply to demand.
The main takeaway from our work is that
it is important for film distributors to understand the role of word-of-mouth in determining film success, and the role of advertising in influencing word-of-mouth.
the survival of a film at the box office is a function of its own performance as well as the unobserved heterogeneity between films.
the Australian box-office environment is characterised by a strong word-of-mouth component, and that this component is a major determinant of film survival.
